title: Conjunctive Queries: A Query Describes a Pattern
lead: Evaluating a conjunctive query means finding assignments to its variables that make every relational condition true.
goals: Translate SQL or relational algebra into a conjunctive query
Distinguish output variables from existentially quantified variables
Find homomorphisms and determine the result set

sections.title: A small language with precise meaning
sections.html:
Which students take a course taught by Linh? To answer, we need two pieces of evidence: a student's enrolment and Linh teaching that same course. Finding each fact somewhere in the database is insufficient. The course values must agree.

Use this original example throughout the lesson:

Enrol(student,course)       Teach(teacher,course)
An   DB                     Linh DB
Bao  AI                     Minh AI
Chi  DB

First filter Teach to Linh: {(Linh,DB)}. Join that with Enrol on course: {(An,DB,Linh),(Chi,DB,Linh)}. Finally keep student: {An,Chi}. These are selection, join and projection respectively. We have described an answer by a sequence of relational-algebra operations.

We can instead describe the evidence an answer needs: Q(s) :- Enrol(s,c), Teach('Linh',c). Read it as “return s if some c makes both facts true.” The comma means AND. The two appearances of c demand the same course. Quoted 'Linh' is a fixed value; s and c are variables whose values we must find.

This is a conjunctive query, or CQ: a pattern built from relational conditions joined by AND. Each condition is an atom; the part after :- is the body. The head Q(s) names the output. The non-output variable c is existential: it must have a witness, but its value is hidden in the answer.

The calculus expression {s | ∃c (Enrol(s,c) ∧ Teach('Linh',c))} states the same requirement. Codd's theorem connects the expressive power of relational algebra and domain-independent relational calculus; it does not assert equal running times. Domain independence means unrelated extra domain values cannot alter this answer. Here every output variable is bound by a body fact, so an arbitrary new name cannot become an answer by itself.

Basic CQs capture the positive equality/selection/projection/join fragment. Negation, arbitrary OR and universal quantification are outside this language. We use sets and no NULL: each answer occurs once. SQL usually uses bags, so we will explicitly add DISTINCT when comparing it with this model.

sections.title: Worked example: who takes a course taught by Linh?
sections.html:
Let us execute the pattern rather than memorize its notation. Start with the same Enrol and Teach facts. Each enrolment proposes values for s and c; the second atom either confirms or rejects them.

Proposed assignmentRequired teaching factDecision
s=An, c=DBTeach('Linh',DB)Present: output An
s=Bao, c=AITeach('Linh',AI)Absent: reject
s=Chi, c=DBTeach('Linh',DB)Present: output Chi

The answer is {An,Chi}. Teach('Minh',AI) does not rescue Bao: the query asks for Linh, and a constant cannot be replaced to make a match work.

SELECT DISTINCT e.student
FROM Enrol e JOIN Teach t ON e.course=t.course
WHERE t.teacher='Linh';

The ON condition performs the shared-c check; WHERE enforces the constant; SELECT keeps s; DISTINCT supplies set semantics. In algebra the same stages are π_student(Enrol ⋈_{Enrol.course=Teach.course} σ_{teacher='Linh'}(Teach)). These translations describe the same result, while the optimizer may choose a different execution order.

Now change the original example to Enrol={(A,DB),(A,AI),(B,AI)} and Teach={(Linh,DB),(Linh,AI)}. The complete matches are (s=A,c=DB), (s=A,c=AI), (s=B,c=AI). Projecting to s first produces A,A,B; treating the result as a set gives {A,B}. There are three witnesses but only two answers.

Try it: put c in the head. What changes?

Q(s,c) returns {(A,DB),(A,AI),(B,AI)}. The two witnesses for A now produce different output tuples because course is visible. SQL without DISTINCT can retain A twice in the earlier one-column query, which is a different result contract.

sections.title: A homomorphism uses one consistent assignment
sections.html:
We need a precise rule for “one match,” because checking each atom independently can give a false answer. Consider Bao: Enrol(Bao,AI) exists and Teach(Linh,DB) exists, but these facts disagree on c. Together they do not satisfy our pattern.

Write an assignment h={s↦An,c↦DB}. Apply it to the entire body, keeping the constant Linh unchanged:

Enrol(s,c)       → Enrol(An,DB)       ✓
Teach('Linh',c)  → Teach('Linh',DB)   ✓
Q(s)            → Q(An)

Every substituted fact is present, so h is a valid match. Such a structure-preserving assignment is called a homomorphism. The name comes after the operation: substitute consistently, preserve constants, check every atom, then read the head.

For h={s↦Bao,c↦AI}, the first check passes and the second fails. We cannot silently use c=DB only in Teach. Nor can we map the constant Linh to Minh. The same variable has one value throughout an assignment, while constants keep their own values.

Different variables are allowed to share a value. For Q(x,y) :- Pair(x,y) and Pair(a,a), the assignment x=a,y=a is valid. A homomorphism is not required to be one-to-one. Conversely, a repeated variable imposes equality even without an explicit equals sign.

Try it: does Pair(a,b) match Pair(x,x)?

No, if a and b are different values. The first position demands x=a and the second x=b. A single assignment cannot satisfy both. Pair(a,a) does match, with x=a. Test the repeated variable before collecting any output.

Key takeaway

A homomorphism must use a single consistent assignment across the entire body. Preserve constants and every occurrence of each variable. Checking atoms separately with incompatible assignments does not establish a match.

sections.title: Repeated variables and multiple witnesses
sections.html:
Keep Pair={(a,a),(a,b),(b,b)}. We will distinguish an assignment from an output tuple by writing down both.

QueryValid assignmentsOutput set
Q(x) :- Pair(x,x)x=a; x=b{a,b}
Q(x) :- Pair(x,y)(a,a); (a,b); (b,b){a,b}
Q(x,y) :- Pair(x,y)(a,a); (a,b); (b,b){(a,a),(a,b),(b,b)}

The first two queries happen to return the same set on this database, but their requirements differ. The first demands a self-pair. The second allows any partner and then hides that partner. Equality on one database does not prove equivalence on every database.

In the second row, a has two witnesses, y=a and y=b. Projection hides y, so both produce the same head tuple (a). Set semantics retains that tuple once. Counting matches would answer a different question from enumerating CQ answers.

Try it on new data: Pair={(a,b)}. Do the first two queries still agree?

No. Pair(x,x) has no match, so its answer is empty. Pair(x,y) has x=a,y=b and returns {a}. This counterexample explains why repeated variables cannot be discarded merely because an earlier test produced the same answer.

Key takeaway

Multiple witnesses do not duplicate an answer under set semantics. A witness is an assignment showing that the body is true. The result retains only the tuple of head values and removes duplicate tuples.

sections.title: Practice and worked solution
sections.html:
Now transfer the matching rule to a path. Let Link={(a,b),(b,c),(a,c)} and ask Q(x,z) :- Link(x,y), Link(y,z). The same y must be the end of the first edge and the start of the second. This asks for exactly two consecutive edges, rather than a direct edge or an arbitrary-length route.

First edgeRequired second-edge startSecond edgesHead
(a,b)b(b,c)(a,c)
(b,c)cNoneNone
(a,c)cNoneNone

The result is {(a,c)}, witnessed by y=b. The direct Link(a,c) fact alone does not satisfy the two-atom body.

Try it: add Link(c,c), and enumerate all witnesses before removing duplicates.

The first edge (a,b) still pairs with (b,c), producing (a,c). Edge (b,c) pairs with (c,c), producing (b,c). Edge (a,c) pairs with (c,c), producing a second (a,c). Finally (c,c) pairs with itself, producing (c,c). Four assignments yield the three-tuple set {(a,c),(b,c),(c,c)}. Different edge occurrences may use the same database fact; the CQ does not require distinct edges.

If the head is empty, Q() :- Link(x,y), Link(y,z), we only ask whether any witness exists. This is a Boolean query. The answer is {()}, the singleton containing the empty tuple, for YES; the empty set means NO. It neither counts paths nor returns their endpoints.

Try it: what if the only fact is Link(c,c)?

The Boolean answer is still YES. Assign x=y=z=c and use that fact in both atom occurrences. Q(x,z) returns {(c,c)}. Requiring distinct nodes would need extra conditions outside this basic pattern.

quiz.question: In Q(x) :- R(x,y), S(y), what is y?
options: An existentially quantified variable shared by the two atoms
quiz.explanation: The variable y does not appear in the head, but every occurrence of y must receive the same value within an assignment.

source.summary: Lecture 23 connects relational algebra and calculus with conjunctive queries. It defines head and body syntax, homomorphisms, and result semantics in terms of matches.
